l: fruit trees, Deuteronomy
s: Fruit trees near a besieged city are protected: Israel may eat from them, so they must not be cut down with an ax. The text asks if a field tree is a man; only known non-food trees may become bulwarks.

l: slain man (found in the field), Deuteronomy
s: He is found dead in a field in the land, and it is not known who struck him. The elders measure from him to the surrounding cities to determine the nearest one, which then bears responsibility for the ritual.

l: elders of the nearest city, Deuteronomy
s: The elders of the city nearest a slain man found in a field, determined by measuring, provide an unworked heifer, break its neck in a valley with running water, wash hands, declare innocence, and receive forgiveness for Israel.

l: heifer, Deuteronomy
s: A ritual heifer from the herd, required to be never worked or yoked; elders bring it to an unplowed, unsown valley with running water, break its neck, and wash their hands over it.

l: heifer ritual for unsolved murder, Deuteronomy
s: purpose forgiveness of innocent blood [elders wash hands and declare innocence] When a slain man is found and the killer unknown, the elders and judges measure to the nearest city, whose elders break an unworked heifer's neck in an uncultivated valley with running water. The priests come near, the elders wash their hands and make their declaration and prayer, and the blood is forgiven, putting away innocent blood.

l: captive woman, Deuteronomy
s: A beautiful woman taken captive in battle may be brought into her captor's house as his wife. She shaves her head, trims her nails, removes captive's clothing, and mourns her parents a full month before marriage. If he has no delight in her, he must release her freely, never selling or enslaving her, since he humbled her.

l: warrior/captor, Deuteronomy
s: A man who goes to battle and sees a beautiful captive woman he desires may take her as his wife after she has mourned a month. If he later has no delight in her, he must let her go free and may not sell her for money or deal with her as a slave.

l: man with two wives, Deuteronomy
s: has_wife hated wife [the other wife is beloved] He has one beloved wife and one hated wife, both of whom have borne him sons. When he divides his inheritance, he may not give the beloved wife's son the firstborn's rights over the hated wife's firstborn, but must acknowledge the true firstborn.

l: hated wife, Deuteronomy
s: is_mother_of firstborn son of the hated wife She is the less-loved of a man's two wives and has borne him children, including his firstborn son. Her status does not change her son's right as firstborn.

l: firstborn son of the hated wife, Deuteronomy
s: has_right firstborn's double portion inheritance [must be acknowledged by the father] Though his mother is the hated wife, he is the firstborn and his father must acknowledge him as such. He is called the beginning of his father's strength, and the right of the firstborn is his.

l: firstborn's double portion inheritance, Deuteronomy
s: is_a right of the firstborn [double portion of all the father has] The father must give the acknowledged firstborn a double portion of all he has. This applies even when the firstborn is the son of the hated wife, and it may not be given instead to the beloved wife's son.

l: stubborn and rebellious son, Deuteronomy
s: A son who refuses to obey his father or mother, even when chastened. His parents bring him to the city elders, accusing him of being stubborn, rebellious, a glutton and drunkard; the men stone him to death, removing evil.

l: parents of the rebellious son, Deuteronomy
s: bring_before elders of the nearest city [to accuse the son at the gate] After chastening fails, the father and mother take hold of their son and bring him to the elders of his city at the gate. They state that he is stubborn, rebellious, will not obey, and is a glutton and drunkard.

l: man put to death and hanged, Deuteronomy
s: A man guilty of a capital sin is executed and hanged on a tree; being accursed of God, his body must be buried the same day, not left overnight, lest it defile the land.

l: brother (the neighbor of the addressee), Deuteronomy
s: owns ox [may go astray or fall by the way] owns donkey [may be lost or fall down]

l: lost animals and property (brother's ox, sheep, donkey, garment), Deuteronomy
s: must_be_returned_to brother (the neighbor of the addressee) [kept at the finder's house until the owner seeks it]

l: husband (man who accuses his wife), Deuteronomy
s: A husband who falsely accuses his wife must pay her father one hundred silver shekels and may never divorce her.

l: young lady (accused wife), Deuteronomy
s: is_wife_of husband (man who accuses his wife) [given by her father]

l: father of the young lady, Deuteronomy
s: is_father_of young lady (accused wife) The young lady's father, with her mother, brings the tokens of her virginity to the elders at the gate and states that he gave his daughter to the man, who now hates her. If the accusation is proved false, he receives the fine of one hundred shekels. In the case of an unbetrothed virgin seized, he receives fifty shekels from the man.

l: elders of the city, Deuteronomy
s: judge_case_at city gate [hear the accusation against the wife] The elders of the city sit at the gate and hear the dispute over the accused wife. The cloth is spread before them. If the husband is found false, they take him and chastise him and fine him one hundred shekels of silver.

l: tokens of virginity, Deuteronomy
s: are_presented_to elders of the city [by the young lady's parents, at the gate] The tokens of virginity are the cloth the young lady's parents bring and spread before the elders to refute the husband's charge. Their presence clears her and condemns him. If they were not found in her, she is stoned.

l: adultery with a married woman (case), Deuteronomy
s: has_penalty death [both the man and the woman] If a man is found lying with a woman married to a husband, both the man and the woman must die. This removes the evil from Israel.

l: man and betrothed virgin in the city (case), Deuteronomy
s: has_penalty stoning [both die; she did not cry out in the city] If a man finds a betrothed virgin in the city and lies with her, both are brought to the city gate and stoned. She dies because she did not cry out in the city, and he because he humbled his neighbor's wife. This removes the evil from among them.

l: rape of a betrothed woman in the field (case), Deuteronomy
s: has_penalty death of the man only [the woman is not guilty] If a man finds a betrothed lady in the field and forces her, only the man dies. She is to be left unpunished, having no sin worthy of death, because she cried out and no one was there to save her. The case is compared to a man rising against his neighbor and killing him.

l: unbetrothed virgin seized (case), Deuteronomy
s: A legal case where a man seizes an unbetrothed virgin and lies with her and they are found; he must pay her father fifty shekels of silver, then marry her and never divorce her.

l: the LORD's assembly, Deuteronomy
s: The LORD's assembly is closed to the emasculated, to those born of a forbidden union, and to Ammonites and Moabites, with the restriction lasting to the tenth generation. The children of Edomites and Egyptians may enter in the third generation.

l: Ammonite, Deuteronomy
s: Ammonites are a group barred from the LORD's assembly to the tenth generation, forever, for withholding bread and water from Israel leaving Egypt and hiring Balaam to curse them; Israelites must never seek their peace or prosperity.

l: Moabite, Deuteronomy
s: Moabites are a group permanently barred from the LORD's assembly to the tenth generation for withholding bread and water from Israel and hiring Balaam to curse them; Israelites must never seek their peace or prosperity.

l: military camp, Deuteronomy
s: The Israelite military camp is holy because the LORD walks in its midst. Soldiers must avoid every evil thing: the unclean stay outside until evening, bathe, and return at sundown, and waste goes outside the camp, covered with a trowel.

l: escaped servant, Deuteronomy
s: An escaped servant who flees his master to the Israelites: they must not return him to the master, and he may live among them in any gate-town he chooses, where it pleases him, without being oppressed.

l: prostitution, Deuteronomy
s: Prostitution is a practice forbidden among Israelite daughters and sons. Its hire or wages, including a male prostitute's, may not be brought into the LORD's house for any vow, being declared an abomination to the LORD.

l: interest lending, Deuteronomy
s: Interest lending is forbidden toward fellow Israelites on money, food, or anything lent, but permitted toward foreigners; obeying the brother rule is linked to the LORD's blessing in the land.

l: vows, Deuteronomy
s: Vows to the LORD are a topic of obligation: a vow must be paid without delay because the LORD will require it and delay is sin, though choosing not to vow is no sin.

l: neighbor's vineyard and grain, Deuteronomy
s: A rule on entering a neighbor's vineyard and grain: one may eat grapes freely or pluck ears by hand, but may not carry grapes away in a container or use a sickle on standing grain.

l: husband (the man who divorces his wife), Deuteronomy
s: A husband who finds some unseemly thing in his wife may write her a certificate of divorce, put it in her hand, and send her out of his house. If she later marries another man and is divorced or widowed, he may not take her again as wife. A newly married man is exempt from the army and business for one year to cheer his wife.

l: wife (the divorced woman), Deuteronomy
s: The wife who finds no favor is given a certificate of divorce and sent out of the house. After leaving she may become another man's wife. If her second husband divorces her or dies, she is considered defiled with respect to her first husband, who may not take her back.

l: divorce, Deuteronomy
s: requires certificate of divorce [written by the husband and put in the wife's hand] Divorce is done by writing a certificate, placing it in the wife's hand, and sending her from the house. It frees her to marry another man. If a second marriage ends by divorce or death, the first husband may not remarry her, since that is an abomination to the LORD.

l: pledge, Deuteronomy
s: Pledge regulations in Chapter 24 protect borrowers: mills or upper millstones cannot be taken because they take a life in pledge, nor a widow's clothing. Lenders must wait outside rather than enter the house, and a poor man's garment must be returned by sunset, earning blessing and righteousness.

l: lender, Deuteronomy
s: A lender, bound by rules about collecting pledges: he must not enter a neighbor's house but wait outside, and must not keep a poor man's pledge overnight, returning it at sundown, which counts as righteousness.

l: neighbor (the borrower), Deuteronomy
s: brings_pledge_to lender [outside the house] The neighbor who borrows brings the pledge outside to the lender rather than having his house entered. If poor, he gets his garment pledge back at sundown so he may sleep in it. He then blesses the lender.

l: hired servant, Deuteronomy
s: A poor, needy hired servant, whether brother or foreigner, must not be oppressed. He is owed his wages the same day before sunset, since he depends on them; otherwise he may cry out to the LORD, and it would be sin.

l: fatherless, Deuteronomy
s: is_entitled_to justice [may not be deprived of it] The fatherless must not be deprived of justice. Sheaves forgotten in the field, olives remaining on the boughs, and vineyard gleanings are left for them. The commands are grounded in Israel's memory of slavery in Egypt.

l: widow, Deuteronomy
s: is_protected_from clothing taken in pledge A widow's clothing may not be taken in pledge, and she must not be deprived of justice. Forgotten sheaves, remaining olives, and vineyard gleanings are left for her. The LORD will bless the work of those who do so.

l: gleaning harvest (sheaf, olives, vineyard), Deuteronomy
s: A harvest law in Chapter 24: forgotten sheaves, olive boughs, and vineyard gleanings must not be gathered a second time. They are reserved for the foreigner, fatherless, and widow, and the LORD promises to bless the owner's work for obeying.

l: Amalek, Deuteronomy
s: Amalek is a group that, lacking fear of God, attacked Israel on the way out of Egypt, striking the feeble rearmost who were faint and weary; Israel is commanded to remember this and, once at rest, blot out its memory.

l: levirate marriage, Deuteronomy
s: Levirate marriage is a duty when brothers dwell together and one dies sonless: the surviving brother must marry the widow rather than a stranger, and her firstborn succeeds in the dead man's name, preserving it in Israel.

l: dead brother, Deuteronomy
s: has_status childless The brother who dies without a son is to have his name preserved in Israel through the firstborn son born to his widow and his brother. This son succeeds in his name so it will not be blotted out.

l: widow, Deuteronomy
s: A childless man's widow, wife of his dead brother, may not marry a stranger; if her brother-in-law refuses her, she appeals to the elders at the gate, who witness her removing his sandal and spitting.

l: surviving brother, Deuteronomy
s: A surviving brother, husband's brother of a widow, is obligated to marry her. If he refuses after the elders speak to him, his sandal is loosed and she spits on him, and his house is named 'The house of him who had his sandal removed.'

l: sandal removal ritual, Deuteronomy
s: A shaming ritual in which a widow, before the elders, removes the sandal of a surviving brother who refuses levirate duty and spits in his face, leaving his house with a shameful name in Israel.

l: honest weights and measures, Deuteronomy
s: Honest weights and measures: Israel is commanded to keep perfect and just ones, not diverse heavy and light, large and small. Obedience promises long days in the land; unrighteous dealing is an abomination to the LORD.

l: priest, Deuteronomy
s: receives first fruits offering [takes the basket from the worshiper] The priest serving in those days receives the worshipper's profession that he has come into the promised land. He takes the basket from the worshipper's hand and sets it down before the altar of the LORD.

l: first fruits offering, Deuteronomy
s: The first fruits offering is the first of the ground's fruit, carried in a basket to the place the LORD chooses. The priest sets it before the altar, the worshipper recites a confession and worships, then rejoices in the LORD's goodness, sharing with the Levite and foreigner.

l: tithe of the third year, Deuteronomy
s: A tithing event in the third year, the year of tithing: the people complete tithing all their increase and give it to the Levite, foreigner, fatherless, and widow to eat and be filled, then declare before the LORD that the holy things were handled properly.

l: Joseph, Deuteronomy
s: Joseph is a figure whose land Moses declares blessed by the LORD with heavenly dew, the deep, sun and moon fruits, ancient mountains, and earth's fullness. Though separated from his brothers, the blessing rests on his head. His majesty, like a firstborn ox with horns, overcomes peoples through Ephraim's ten thousands and Manasseh's thousands.

l: plastered stones (stones inscribed with the law), Deuteronomy
s: Great stones to be set up on Mount Ebal after Israel crosses the Jordan, coated with plaster, and inscribed very plainly with all the words of the law.

l: law, Deuteronomy
s: The law is to be written in full, very plainly, on plastered stones on Mount Ebal. The final curse pronounces a curse on anyone who does not uphold its words by doing them, and the people answer 'Amen'.

l: altar (altar to the LORD on Mount Ebal), Deuteronomy
s: An altar to the LORD on Mount Ebal, built by Israel from uncut stones with no iron tool, for burnt and peace offerings, where people eat and rejoice before the LORD.

l: curses, Deuteronomy
s: The curses are covenant penalties tied to disobedience, not listening to the LORD's voice. In chapter 27 the Levites declare twelve of them aloud, covering secret idolatry, dishonoring parents, moving a landmark, misleading the blind, withholding justice from the foreigner, fatherless, and widow, sexual offenses, secret murder, bribery to kill the innocent, and failing to uphold the law, with all the people answering 'Amen.' Chapter 28 reverses the blessings at greater length: confusion, disease, drought, defeat, loss, foreign domination, siege cannibalism, and exile, pursuing the people until destroyed, serving as a sign and wonder forever.

l: distant nation, Deuteronomy
s: A distant nation from the end of the earth, brought by the LORD against the Israelites. Swift as an eagle, with an incomprehensible language and a fierce, merciless disposition, it devours livestock and crops, besieges every gate until fortified walls fall, and leaves no grain, wine, or oil.

l: exile and scattering among nations, Deuteronomy
s: The exile and scattering of the Israelites among the nations is a judgment the LORD brings, driving them and their king from one end of the earth to the other. In Chapter 28 it means serving wood and stone gods, becoming an astonishment, proverb and byword, and living with no rest, trembling hearts, failing eyes and constant fear. Chapter 30 turns to restoration: if they remember, return and obey with all heart and soul, the LORD releases them, gathers them, returns them to the land, circumcises their hearts, and prospers them.

l: covenant of Moab, Deuteronomy
s: The covenant of Moab is a covenant made in Moab, in addition to Horeb's, sworn by the LORD to establish Israel as his people as promised to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. It binds present and future generations; keeping it brings prosperity, while abandoning it explains the land's ruin.

l: curses of the covenant, Deuteronomy
s: is_written_in the law [book of the law] The curses are written in this book of the law and are said to fall on anyone who hears them yet blesses himself in his heart while walking in stubbornness. They would set that person apart for evil out of all the tribes and blot out his name. They are also the cause of the LORD's anger burning against the land and the uprooting of the people.

l: idolatrous individual (among Israel), Deuteronomy
s: An idolatrous individual, whether man, woman, family, or tribe, whose heart turns from the LORD to serve other gods, likened to a root producing bitter poison. Hearing the covenant curse, he blesses himself and assumes peace despite stubbornness; the LORD refuses pardon, his anger burns, and the name is blotted out.

l: devastated land, Deuteronomy
s: A land foretold as devastated: plagues, sulfur, salt, burning, unsown and barren like Sodom, Gomorrah, Admah, and Zeboiim. Future peoples will ask why the LORD did this, and be told the people abandoned the covenant and served other gods, so the LORD uprooted them.

l: life and death choice, Deuteronomy
s: has_witness heaven and earth [called to witness against Israelites] The speaker sets before the Israelites life and prosperity on one side and death and evil on the other, and calls heaven and earth as witnesses. Loving and obeying the LORD leads to life, multiplication, and blessing in the land, while turning away to other gods means certain perishing. The Israelites are urged to choose life, for themselves and their descendants, by loving the LORD, obeying his voice, and clinging to him.

l: song (Moses' song), Deuteronomy
s: The LORD tells Moses to write the song and teach it to Israel as a witness against them, since it will not be forgotten by their descendants. Moses writes it the same day, teaches it to the people, and speaks its words to the whole assembly.

l: strange gods (Israel's idols), Deuteronomy
s: is_a demons, not God [new gods unknown to the fathers] The strange gods are described as demons and not God, new gods that arose recently, unknown to Israel and not dreaded by their fathers. Their worship provoked the LORD to jealousy and anger. The LORD mocks them, asking where these gods are and challenging them to rise up and protect Israel, since the one who ate their sacrifices cannot save them.

l: Song of Moses, Deuteronomy
s: has_purpose witness to the law [Moses's exhortation that follows it] The song is a poem beginning with a call to heaven and earth to hear. It praises the LORD as the faithful Rock, recounts his care for Israel, accuses Israel of apostasy, announces judgment and later vengeance on adversaries, and ends with the nations invited to rejoice. Moses and Joshua recite it to the people, and Moses tells them to take all its words to heart.

l: divine judgment and vengeance, Deuteronomy
s: belongs_to the LORD [vengeance and recompense] The LORD announces judgment on Israel through fire, hunger, burning heat, wild beasts, venom, and the sword, which will bring terror to young and old alike. He restrains total destruction so the enemy cannot boast, then declares that vengeance and recompense are his and that he will repay his adversaries with his sword. The song closes with the promise that he will avenge his servants' blood and make atonement for his land and people.

l: Israel's apostasy, Deuteronomy
s: has_consequence the LORD's anger [hides his face, kindles fire] Israel is accused of dealing corruptly, forgetting the Rock who bore them, and rejecting the God of their salvation after growing prosperous. They provoked the LORD to jealousy with strange gods, abominations, and sacrifices to demons. This apostasy leads the LORD to hide his face and bring calamity, and to provoke Israel in turn with a foolish nation that is not a people.

l: blessing of Moses, Deuteronomy
s: Moses' blessing, given to the children of Israel before his death, fills chapter 33: it opens praising the LORD's coming and the law, addresses each tribe in turn, and closes praising God and saved Israel.

l: plains of Moab, Deuteronomy
s: The plains of Moab are the place from which Moses departs to ascend Mount Nebo. The children of Israel weep for him there for thirty days.

l: Moses' death and burial, Deuteronomy
s: Moses dies at age one hundred twenty in the land of Moab, according to the LORD's word, and is buried in a valley opposite Beth Peor; his tomb's location remains unknown today.

l: The Book of Isaiah
s: This is the Book of Isaiah, 66 chapters of prophecy by Isaiah son of Amoz concerning Judah and Jerusalem, set from the reigns of Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz and Hezekiah onward. It moves from judgment to comfort to restoration. Chapters 1-12 open with the LORD accusing a rebellious, bloodstained people, offering cleansing if they obey, and promising a purged Zion. Isaiah's call comes in the year Uzziah died, when he sees the Lord enthroned and is sent to a people who will not understand. Under Ahaz, the Immanuel sign is given amid the Syrian-Israelite threat, and Assyria is foretold as a flood. Promises follow of a child with the names Wonderful Counselor and Prince of Peace and a shoot from Jesse's stock bringing universal peace, ending in a song of thanksgiving. Chapters 13-27 are oracles against nations: Babylon, Moab, Damascus, Egypt, Tyre and others, with Assyria also broken. Egypt and Assyria are eventually joined in worship with Israel. The oracles widen into judgment on the whole earth, a feast on the LORD's mountain, death swallowed up, and songs of trust. Chapters 28-35 pronounce woes on scoffers and on those who rely on Egypt rather than the Holy One of Israel. They promise a righteous king, Assyria's fall, and a wilderness that blossoms with a Holy Way for the redeemed, while Edom is laid waste. Chapters 36-39 are narrative. Sennacherib's envoy Rabshakeh taunts Jerusalem, Hezekiah prays, and the LORD's angel strikes 185,000 Assyrians. Hezekiah then recovers from illness with fifteen added years, but shows Babylon's envoys his treasures and is told they will be carried to Babylon. Chapters 40-55 shift to comfort for exiles. The LORD, incomparable Creator, mocks idols and names Cyrus as his anointed to free Israel. Babylon is condemned. A servant is called as a light to the nations, suffers, and bears the sins of many. The LORD invites all to come and promises his word will accomplish what he pleases. Chapters 56-66 call for justice, true fasting and Sabbath-keeping, and welcome foreigners and eunuchs. They confess the people's sin, and Zion is told to arise and shine as nations bring wealth. An anointed speaker proclaims good news, and the LORD comes in vengeance. The people pray for his return, and he promises new heavens and a new earth where weeping ends and wolf and lamb feed together. The book closes with all flesh worshipping before him and the fate of transgressors, whose worm and fire never end.

l: Isaiah, The Book of Isaiah
s: Isaiah, son of Amoz, is a prophet and servant of the LORD who saw visions concerning Judah and Jerusalem during the reigns of Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah. His story begins with a call: seeing the Lord on a throne, he declares himself undone, a man of unclean lips living among a people of unclean lips. A seraph touches his mouth with a live coal, his iniquity is taken away and sin forgiven, and when asked who will go he volunteers, 'Here I am. Send me!' He is told to deliver a message this people will not understand, and asks 'Lord, how long?' He is then commanded to meet King Ahaz with his son Shearjashub, telling him to keep calm and not fear Rezin and the son of Remaliah, whose plot will not stand. He fathers a son named Maher Shalal Hash Baz, is warned not to walk in the way of this people, seals the law among his disciples, and resolves to wait for the LORD. He and the children given him are signs and wonders in Israel. He also saw the burden of Babylon as a vision. At the LORD's command he walks naked and barefoot for three years as a sign concerning Egypt and Ethiopia. Under Hezekiah he reassures envoys about the Assyrian king, relays the LORD's condemnation of Sennacherib, and promises the city will be defended. He tells Hezekiah he will die, then returns with fifteen more years and a fig poultice for the boil. Finally he questions Hezekiah about visitors from Babylon and announces that his possessions and some of his sons will be taken there. Across the records he is a messenger who obeys, bearing the LORD's word to kings.

l: Judah, The Book of Isaiah
s: Judah is a land and people, called Immanuel's land, whose fortunes swing from ruin to restoration. It begins fallen: with Jerusalem it loses supply, support and leadership because its words and deeds provoke the LORD's glory. Syria and Ephraim plot against it but fail, yet Assyria is foretold to overrun it like a flood, leaving briers, thorns and lost vineyards. Later its dispersed are gathered from the four corners, persecutors are cut off, and with Ephraim it plunders and rules neighboring peoples. Finally it is the land where the song of a strong city is sung, and it becomes a terror to Egypt.

l: Jerusalem, The Book of Isaiah
s: Jerusalem, paired with Judah and Mount Zion, is the city at the center of these records: a place that is both a literal location and a people (its sons, remnant, and inhabitants). It is the site of the LORD's work, the source of his word in the latter days, and the object of judgment, threat, comfort, and restoration. Most important is its movement from ruin to renewal. Early on it is ruined for its tongue and doings against the LORD, stripped of supplies and leaders, with gates lamenting as she sits desolate on the ground. Yet those who remain, written among the living, will be called holy, and its blood will be purged by the spirit of justice and burning. Under Assyrian pressure, the Lord says he will complete his work on Mount Zion and Jerusalem, and Jerusalem is fortified, with houses broken down for the wall and a reservoir made. Rabshakeh comes with an army and mocks the idea that the LORD would deliver it, but the LORD promises to protect and preserve the city for his own sake and David's: the king of Assyria will not enter, shoot an arrow, or cast up a mound. Then the tone turns to comfort: her warfare is accomplished and her iniquity pardoned, she has received double for her sins, and she will be inhabited and built, with the temple's foundation laid. She has drunk and drained the cup of the LORD's wrath, has no sons to guide her, and suffers desolation, but the LORD takes the cup away and she will not drink it again. Called the holy city, she is told to put on beautiful garments, shake off the dust, and sit up, since the uncircumcised and unclean will no longer enter; the LORD has comforted and redeemed her. Watchmen are set on her walls, and she will be a praise on the earth, called Sought Out, A City Not Forsaken. After a lament that she is a desolation, the LORD promises to create her as a delight and her people a joy, with no more weeping. The records end with peace extended to her like a river, comfort like a mother's, and her holy mountain as the place where all flesh comes to worship.

l: Ahaz, The Book of Isaiah
s: Ahaz, king of Judah, son of Jotham and descendant of David's house, trembles when told Syria allies with Ephraim. Though the LORD, through Isaiah, offers a sign, he refuses, saying he won't tempt the LORD. The LORD then foretells trouble, including Assyria's king, for him, his people, and his father's house.

l: Hezekiah, The Book of Isaiah
s: Hezekiah is a king of Judah, a descendant of David who removed high places and altars and commanded worship before one altar. The records follow him through four crises. In the fourteenth year of his reign, Assyria captures Judah's fortified cities and Rabshakeh mocks his trust in the LORD; Hezekiah tears his clothes, wears sackcloth, goes to the LORD's house, sends to Isaiah, and spreads Sennacherib's letter before the LORD, praying for deliverance. The LORD defends the city for his own sake and David's. When Hezekiah is sick and near death, he prays and weeps; the LORD grants fifteen more years and forgives his sins. He resolves to walk carefully and worship in the LORD's house all his life. Pleased by Babylon's letters and gift, he shows the envoys all his treasures, silver, gold, spices, oil, and armor. Isaiah announces coming loss, yet Hezekiah calls the word good, expecting peace and truth in his days.

l: the LORD, The Book of Isaiah
s: The LORD, also called LORD of Armies and the Holy One of Israel, is the central divine figure of these records, and the records present him as a God rather than a human individual. He raised Israel as children, yet they rebelled. He rejects empty sacrifices and demands justice and righteousness. He is Creator of heaven and earth, the first and the last, the only God and Savior, who declares the end from the beginning. He is also Redeemer, King, Rock, Father and potter. He dwells on Mount Zion, sits enthroned and holy, and is named Zion's judge, lawgiver and king. The account unfolds in phases. First he accuses Judah and Jerusalem. He strips away bread, water and leaders and treats Israel as his vineyard, finding oppression instead of justice. He sends Assyria as the rod of his anger, gives the Immanuel sign, and leaves a small remnant. He then speaks judgments on Babylon, Moab, Damascus, Egypt, Tyre and Edom, and on the earth and its kings. Yet he promises that Egypt, Assyria and Israel will be blessed as his people, his handiwork and his inheritance. In the Hezekiah episodes he defends Jerusalem for his own sake and David's, and his angel strikes the Assyrian camp. He also foretells exile to Babylon. The later chapters turn to comfort. He is the incomparable Creator who never tires and strengthens the weak. He chooses Israel and his servant, anoints Cyrus, forgives sins for his own sake, and redeems Jacob. He allows the suffering servant to be bruised and gives him a portion with the great. He promises an everlasting covenant of peace, free pardon, and a place for foreigners and eunuchs on his holy mountain. He dwells with the humble and contrite, and defines the true fast as justice and mercy. He acts as a warrior with his own arm, treading the winepress in anger. Zion becomes his delight, like a bride. The people plead with him as Father, and he creates new heavens and a new earth. He ends by judging all flesh with fire and sword, comforting Jerusalem like a mother, and gathering all nations to see his glory.

l: Israel, The Book of Isaiah
s: Israel is presented in these records as a group, a people and nation, whose story moves from rebellion and ruin to restoration. It begins as a rebellious, sinful nation that lacks knowledge of the LORD, unlike the ox and donkey. It is loaded with iniquity, wounded from foot to head, and has forsaken the LORD. Its country is desolate and its cities burned. Only a very small remnant left by the LORD of Armies keeps it from being like Sodom and Gomorrah. As the LORD's vineyard it was expected to yield justice and righteousness but produced oppression and a cry of distress. Judgment follows. The Syrians in front and the Philistines behind devour it, and the LORD cuts off head and tail in one day. Its leaders, the honorable elder and the lying prophet, lead the people astray, and the people have not sought the One who struck them. Although numerous as the sand of the sea, only a remnant will return, and that remnant will lean on the LORD, the Holy One of Israel, in truth, and need not fear Assyria. The turn comes with promises of the future. The LORD will choose Israel again and set it in its own land. It will rule its oppressors and take captive those who held it captive. It will be third with Egypt and Assyria, a blessing within the earth, and the LORD calls it his inheritance. Israel is named his chosen and servant, for whose sake Cyrus is called. It is described as a new sharp threshing instrument made by the LORD. It is saved with an everlasting salvation, and all its offspring will be justified in the LORD. The LORD is its Redeemer and Holy One, who carried it from birth and will grant it his glory. The closing image is a forsaken wife, barren and widowed, called back by the LORD. She is promised restoration, an enlarged dwelling, establishment in righteousness, distance from oppression and terror, and protection from every weapon formed against her as the heritage of the LORD's servants.

l: Zion, The Book of Isaiah
s: Zion is the LORD's city and mount, treated throughout these records as a place that moves from desolation to glory. It is also addressed as a woman, the "daughter of Zion." It begins in a bleak state: left like a shelter in a vineyard, a hut in a melon field, and a besieged city. The LORD promises to redeem it with justice and righteousness. Those left in it will be called holy and written among the living, and the LORD will wash away its filth and cover the habitation of the mount with a protective canopy. It is founded by the LORD and is a refuge for the afflicted of his people. It is the place of the name of the LORD of Armies, where the Holy One of Israel is great among its people. Jerusalem is part of it, pictured as a quiet habitation like a tent whose stakes will never be plucked up, and as a city of appointed festivals. There the people will weep no more, and wide rivers will carry the LORD's majesty. The ransomed return to it singing. Zion then complains that she is forsaken and forgotten, and the LORD answers that he will not forget her, since her walls are always before him and she is engraved on his hands. Bereaved of her children, she is promised that her land will grow too small for her returning inhabitants. Her wilderness will be made like Eden, and the LORD will say, "You are my people." The captive daughter is urged to awake, free herself from bonds, and hear that her God reigns and is returning. Zion is told to arise and shine. Once forsaken and hated, she becomes an eternal excellency, with walls named Salvation, gates named Praise that stay open continually, and peace and righteousness as her rulers. She is built of sapphires, rubies, and sparkling jewels. She will be called the LORD's City, Hephzibah, and a crown of beauty in the LORD's hand, and her land Beulah. She will no longer be called Forsaken or Desolate. Her salvation shines like a burning lamp, and the LORD delights in her. The final record returns to ruin: Zion has become a wilderness, named among the holy cities lying desolate. This leaves the arc from desolation to restoration closed by a renewed lament.

l: sacrifices and offerings, The Book of Isaiah
s: is_regarded_by_the_lord_as burden [New Moons and appointed feasts] The LORD says he has had enough of burnt offerings of rams, fat of fed animals, and the blood of bulls, lambs, and male goats. He calls vain offerings, incense, New Moons, Sabbaths, and convocations an abomination and a burden because they accompany evil and hands full of blood.

l: sin and judgment, The Book of Isaiah
s: Isaiah 1 presents sin and judgment: the people, burdened with iniquity and scarlet sins, are offered cleansing as white as snow. Yet if they refuse and rebel, the sword devours them; the LORD will avenge, purge dross, and consume those who forsake him unquenchably.

l: justice and righteousness, The Book of Isaiah
s: Justice and righteousness is a theme in Isaiah. In Chapter 1 the LORD commands the people to seek justice, relieve the oppressed, and defend the fatherless and widow, laments a city now full of murderers and bribe-loving princes, and promises restoration and redemption of Zion with justice. In Chapter 42 his servant brings justice to the nations until it is set on earth.

l: house of prayer (the LORD's house), The Book of Isaiah
s: The LORD's house of prayer is a place to be established in the latter days on the top of the mountains, raised above the hills. All nations will flow to it to learn the God of Jacob's ways. There foreigners' offerings will be accepted, and it will be called a house of prayer for all peoples.

l: nations, The Book of Isaiah
s: will_stop war [beat swords into plowshares] The nations will flow to the LORD's mountain, and many peoples will go there to learn his ways and walk in his paths. The LORD will judge between them, and they will beat swords into plowshares and spears into pruning hooks, no longer lifting sword against each other or learning war.

l: house of Jacob, The Book of Isaiah
s: The house of Jacob is a people of the LORD, portrayed across three chapters as both cherished and faulted. It is first urged to walk in the LORD's light, yet described as forsaken: practicing divination like the Philistines, clasping hands with foreigners, and filling its land with silver, gold, horses, chariots, and idols made by its own hands. Next, God calls it to listen, reminding it that he has carried it from birth and will carry and deliver it into old age. Finally it is charged with sin despite daily seeking God, rebuked for oppressing laborers while fasting, and offered restoration and the heritage of Jacob.

l: idols, The Book of Isaiah
s: Idols are objects worshipped throughout the land, made by human hands and fingers; they will utterly pass away, and in that day men will discard their silver and gold idols to moles and bats.

l: Day of the LORD, The Book of Isaiah
s: The Day of the LORD of Armies is a coming day against everything proud, arrogant and lifted up, including cedars of Lebanon, oaks of Bashan, mountains, towers, walls and Tarshish ships; all lofty things are brought low and the LORD alone is exalted.

l: pride and arrogance of man, The Book of Isaiah
s: will_be brought low [in the day of the LORD] The lofty looks and arrogance of men will be bowed down and brought low, as the text states twice. Man is described as brought low and humbled, and the closing verse tells hearers to stop trusting in man, whose breath is in his nostrils.

l: Tarshish, The Book of Isaiah
s: has_possession ships [stronghold laid waste] The ships of Tarshish are called on twice to howl because Tyre's stronghold is laid waste, and the coast dwellers are told to pass over to Tarshish. The daughter of Tarshish is told to pass through her land like the Nile, since there is no restraint any more.

l: men hiding from the LORD, The Book of Isaiah
s: A group of men flee the LORD's terror and majestic glory as he arises to shake the earth. They hide in rock caves, earth holes and clefts, entering the dust, and cast their idols away to moles and bats.

l: daughters of Zion, The Book of Isaiah
s: The daughters of Zion are a group condemned as arrogant, with outstretched necks, flirting eyes and jingling anklets; the Lord punishes them with sores, baldness, and stripped finery, replacing beauty with rottenness, rope, sackcloth and branding.

l: people of Jerusalem and Judah, The Book of Isaiah
s: The people of Jerusalem and Judah act against the Lord in word and deed, openly parading their sin like Sodom. Misled by leaders and oppressed by children as rulers, they suffer mutual oppression; disaster follows, the righteous are told it will be well, and warriors fall by the sword.

l: leaders and elders (of Judah), The Book of Isaiah
s: Leaders and elders of Judah are accused by the LORD in judgment: they eat up the vineyard, hold the poor's plunder in their houses, and grind the poor's faces. Their leadership misleads the people, and their authority is taken away.

l: boys and children (rulers of Judah), The Book of Isaiah
s: The Lord gives boys as princes and children to rule over the people. Children are called the oppressors of the people, and a child behaves proudly against the old man.

l: adornments and finery (of the women of Zion), The Book of Isaiah
s: is_taken_away_by the Lord, GOD of Armies [in that day] A long list of items is named, including anklets, headbands, crescent necklaces, earrings, bracelets, veils, rings, robes, mirrors, tiaras, and shawls. The Lord will take all of them away, and they will be replaced by rottenness, a rope, baldness, sackcloth, and branding.

l: vineyard (the beloved's vineyard), The Book of Isaiah
s: The beloved's vineyard, owned by the LORD of Armies, sits on a very fruitful hill, carefully dug, cleared of stones, planted with the choicest vine, and given a tower and wine press. Despite this care it yields wild grapes. The beloved vows to remove its hedge and wall, leaving it trampled, overgrown with briers and thorns, and without rain. It is finally identified allegorically as the house of Israel and the men of Judah.

l: Judgment and punishment of Judah, The Book of Isaiah
s: includes falling of men by the sword [men and mighty in war] The LORD stands to contend and judge, bringing disaster on the wicked so that the deeds of their hands are paid back to them. The punishment includes loss of food, water, and leaders, oppression, humiliation of the women of Zion, death by the sword, and desolation of Jerusalem. The righteous are told they will eat the fruit of their deeds and that it will be well with them.

l: seven women, The Book of Isaiah
s: Seven women, bearing reproach, seize hold of one man in that day, vowing to supply their own bread and clothing, asking only to be called by his name to remove their reproach.

l: survivors of Israel, The Book of Isaiah
s: part_of Israel The fruit of the land will be the beauty and glory of the survivors of Israel in that day.

l: cloud and smoke (over Mount Zion), The Book of Isaiah
s: A cloud and smoke by day, with flaming fire shining by night, created by the LORD over Mount Zion and her assemblies; it forms a canopy serving as shade from heat and shelter from storm and rain.

l: purification of Jerusalem, The Book of Isaiah
s: The LORD purifies Jerusalem by washing away the filth of Zion's daughters and purging its bloodshed through the spirit of justice and burning, after which the remnant is called holy.

l: men of Judah, The Book of Isaiah
s: is_a pleasant plant of the LORD of Armies The men of Judah, with the inhabitants of Jerusalem, are asked to judge between the beloved and his vineyard. They are named as his pleasant plant, from which he looked for justice and found oppression.

l: Sheol, The Book of Isaiah
s: Sheol is a place beneath that holds departed spirits and has enlarged desire. It stirs to meet the arriving king of Babylon, raising former rulers, who mock his weakness as his pomp falls and worms cover him.

l: those who join house to house (land-grabbers), The Book of Isaiah
s: faces woe [they accumulate land until no room remains] Those who join house to house and lay field to field until there is no room are met with a woe, and are told they will dwell alone in the middle of the land. The LORD says many great and beautiful houses will be desolate and unoccupied, and that ten acres of vineyard will yield only one bath.

l: drunken revelers, The Book of Isaiah
s: A group of drunken revelers who rise early and stay late pursuing strong drink, feasting with music and wine while disregarding the LORD's work. They are met with a woe, and Sheol opens wide to swallow their glory and multitude.

l: those who call evil good (the corrupt and arrogant), The Book of Isaiah
s: A corrupt, arrogant group who invert good and evil, consider themselves wise, and acquit the guilty for bribes while denying the innocent justice. Having rejected the LORD of Armies' law and despised the Holy One's word, they are condemned with woes; their root will rot and their blossom turn to dust.

l: distant nations (invaders), The Book of Isaiah
s: A distant nation summoned by the LORD's banner and whistle arrives swiftly and tirelessly, armed with sharp arrows, bent bows, flint-hoofed horses and whirlwind wheels. They roar like lions, seize prey unopposed, and bring darkness and distress to the land.

l: judgment and desolation, The Book of Isaiah
s: Judgment and desolation: the beloved's vineyard is stripped and laid waste, then houses go desolate, harvests fail, famine, captivity and Sheol claim the proud, people burn like stubble, corpses litter streets, anger unrelenting, ending in invasion and a land of darkness.

l: seraphim, The Book of Isaiah
s: The seraphim are six-winged beings standing above the LORD of Armies in Isaiah's vision. They cry to one another that he is holy and the earth full of his glory; then one touches the narrator's mouth with an altar's live coal, declaring his iniquity removed.

l: this people, The Book of Isaiah
s: A people with unclean lips, addressed by a message they hear without understanding and see without perceiving; hearts fat, ears heavy, eyes shut, so they don't turn and heal. The Lord says they will be removed far away, and even a remaining tenth consumed.

l: Isaiah's commission to a hardening message, The Book of Isaiah
s: Isaiah's commission is a message of hardening: after volunteering when the Lord asks whom to send, he is told to tell this people to hear without understanding, making hearts fat, ears heavy, eyes shut so they do not turn and heal; it lasts until the land is utterly waste.

l: Isaiah's vision of the Lord, The Book of Isaiah
s: In the year King Uzziah died, the narrator sees the Lord enthroned in the temple, his train filling it; seraphim proclaim his holiness, the thresholds shake, smoke fills the house, and the narrator declares himself undone.

l: cleansing of Isaiah's lips, The Book of Isaiah
s: A seraph carries a live coal from the altar with tongs to the narrator, touches it to his mouth, and declares his lips touched, iniquity removed and sin forgiven, answering his cry of unclean lips.

l: coming desolation, The Book of Isaiah
s: Coming desolation is a judgment answering 'how long?': it lasts until cities and houses stand empty and the land is utterly waste, the LORD having removed men far away. Even a surviving tenth is consumed, leaving a stump, the holy seed.

l: Rezin, The Book of Isaiah
s: is_a king of Syria Rezin, king of Syria, went up with Pekah to Jerusalem to war against it but could not prevail. The LORD said his fierce anger is like the smoking tails of torches, and that he is the head of Damascus, which is the head of Syria.

l: Pekah the son of Remaliah, The Book of Isaiah
s: is_a king of Israel Pekah, called the son of Remaliah and king of Israel, joined Rezin in going up against Jerusalem without prevailing. He is described as the head of Samaria and as a co-plotter who planned to tear Judah apart and set up the son of Tabeel as king.

l: Syria, The Book of Isaiah
s: Syria, headed by Damascus under Rezin, allies with Ephraim and plots evil against Judah; the LORD declares the plot will fail, and its remnant will match Israel's glory.

l: Ephraim, The Book of Isaiah
s: Ephraim is a northern people and territory headed by Samaria, whose own head is Remaliah's son. It breaks from Judah, allies with Syria, and joins a plot to divide Judah. Its inhabitants speak with pride and arrogance, vowing to rebuild grander after ruin, and it turns on Manasseh while both oppose Judah. The LORD prophesies it will be broken in pieces within sixty-five years, no longer a people. Its fortress will cease alongside Damascus and Syria's remnant. Its drunkards, wearing a proud crown, face woe, and a mighty one sent by the Lord will trample that crown. Yet one passage foresees envy ending and Ephraim reconciled with Judah, acting together against neighboring peoples.

l: Damascus, The Book of Isaiah
s: Damascus, a city headed by Rezin, is declared in Chapter 17 to lose its kingdom, cease being a city, become a ruinous heap, and be forsaken, left to flocks.

l: Assyria, The Book of Isaiah
s: Assyria is a kingdom, represented chiefly by its proud king, that the records present as the LORD's instrument and later the object of his judgment. It is first foretold as the power the LORD will bring against Ahaz, his people and his father's house, likened to a hired razor and to the mighty flood of the River. It carries off the riches of Damascus and the plunder of Samaria, takes Ashdod through Sargon's commander Tartan, and leads away captives of Egypt and Ethiopia. Called the rod of the Lord's anger, it is sent against a profane nation but does not intend to serve God's purpose. It aims to destroy many nations, boasts of its conquests, compares Samaria to Damascus, advances through towns to Nob and shakes its hand at Jerusalem. It oppresses God's people without cause and lays a yoke and burden on them. The turn comes as the LORD promises to punish its king, burn its forest down to a countable remnant, and break the yoke from Zion's people. He swears to break the Assyrian in his land and tread him on his mountains. A deep burning place, long prepared for the king, is kindled by the LORD's breath. The Assyrian is struck with the rod, falls by a sword not of man, flees, sees his young men put to forced labor and his princes fear the banner. Yet Assyria also appears in restoration: a highway for the remnant, a highway between Egypt and Assyria where they worship together, and the LORD's name for it, 'the work of my hands.'

l: Egypt, The Book of Isaiah
s: Egypt is a land ruled by Pharaoh and described as under a cruel lord, whom the LORD gives it over to. Across the records it is chiefly an unreliable source of refuge. Judah goes down to it for help, trusting its horses, chariots and horsemen, but the LORD calls its help vain, names it Rahab who sits still, and warns of confusion and woe. Rabshakeh likens it to a bruised reed that pierces the hand leaning on it. It is also called a glory in which people hoped, and its captives are to be led away shamed by Assyria. Egypt faces judgment: idols tremble, its heart melts, waters dry up, and its counsel fails. Afterward it is healed, receives a savior, an altar and a pillar to the LORD, is called 'my people,' and is joined with Assyria and Israel. It also serves as the past exodus comparison for a new highway recovering the remnant.

l: the River, The Book of Isaiah
s: The River is a metaphor for invasion: mighty flood waters brought by the Lord on this people, rising over channels and banks, sweeping into Judah up to the neck, wings filling Immanuel's land.

l: Immanuel, The Book of Isaiah
s: Immanuel is a child, the son a virgin will conceive and bear. In chapter 7 he is a sign: before he knows to refuse evil and choose good, the land of the two kings Ahaz abhors is forsaken, and he eats butter and honey. In chapter 9 he is born and given, bearing names Wonderful Counselor, Mighty God, Everlasting Father, and Prince of Peace. Government rests on his shoulders, and he reigns on David's throne forever with justice and righteousness.

l: virgin (the sign), The Book of Isaiah
s: will_bear Immanuel [son] The virgin is said to be the one who will conceive, bear a son, and call his name Immanuel. She is the central figure of the sign the LORD himself gives to the house of David.

l: sign, The Book of Isaiah
s: The LORD told Ahaz to ask a sign in the depth or the height, but Ahaz declined. The LORD then gave the sign himself: the virgin will conceive and bear a son called Immanuel, whose early growth is tied to the forsaking of the land of the two kings.

l: Maher Shalal Hash Baz, The Book of Isaiah
s: Maher Shalal Hash Baz is a symbolic name, instructed by the LORD, for the son of the speaker and the prophetess, written on a large tablet; it signals Assyria will plunder Damascus and Samaria before the child can speak.

l: this people, The Book of Isaiah
s: A people who refuse the gently flowing waters of Shiloah and rejoice in Rezin and Remaliah's son, so a flood will overwhelm them. The speaker is warned not to follow their ways or fear them; without the law, they face hunger, distress, cursing, and thick darkness.

l: covenant and law, The Book of Isaiah
s: is_standard_for this people [no morning for those who do not speak according to it] The speaker is told to wrap up the covenant and seal the law among his disciples. The people are urged to turn to the law and the covenant, and those who do not speak according to this word are said to have no morning.

l: mediums and wizards, The Book of Isaiah
s: has_manner chirp and mutter Those with familiar spirits and wizards, who chirp and mutter, are the ones people urge others to consult. The text rebukes this, asking whether a people should not consult their God instead and whether they should consult the dead on behalf of the living.

l: unjust rulers and decree writers, The Book of Isaiah
s: is_a oppressors of the needy [decree unrighteous decrees] They are met with woe for decreeing unrighteous decrees and writing oppressive ones that deprive the needy of justice and rob the poor of their rights. Through them widows become plunder and the fatherless become prey. They are asked what they will do in the day of visitation, to whom they will flee, and where they will leave their wealth; they will bow down under prisoners and fall among the slain.

l: profane nation (Israel), The Book of Isaiah
s: The profane nation is the people who anger the Lord, against whom he sends Assyria with a command to take plunder and prey and tread them down like the mire of the streets. The text compares its idols to those of the kingdoms Assyria has already found, and the Lord says he will do to Jerusalem and her idols as he did to Samaria. His anger is not turned away and his hand is stretched out still.

l: Assyria's pride and boasting, The Book of Isaiah
s: claims own strength and wisdom [Assyria's boast] Assyria's king claims that all his princes are kings, that he acted by the strength of his hand and his wisdom, removed boundaries, robbed treasures, and gathered the earth like abandoned eggs with no one to chirp. The Lord says he will punish the fruit of his willful proud heart and the insolence of his arrogant looks after finishing his work on Zion and Jerusalem. The boast is answered with a fire that consumes Assyria's glory, fat ones, and forest.

l: ax, saw, rod and staff (tool analogy), The Book of Isaiah
s: illustrates Assyria's subordination to God [tool should not brag against its wielder] The Lord asks whether an ax should brag against the one who chops with it, or a saw exalt itself above the one who saws with it. He adds that a rod lifting those who lift it, or a staff lifting someone who is not wood, would be equally absurd. The analogy shows that Assyria, the rod of his anger, is merely an instrument in his hand and has no ground for boasting.

l: Jesse, The Book of Isaiah
s: Jesse is named as the source of a shoot that will come out of his stock and a branch from his roots that will bear fruit. His root will stand as a banner of the peoples, which the nations will seek, and his resting place will be glorious.

l: shoot (from the stock of Jesse), The Book of Isaiah
s: The shoot is a figure from Jesse's stock, upon whom the LORD's Spirit rests with wisdom, might and fear of the LORD. He delights in that fear, judges the poor and humble with righteousness and equity, wears righteousness as a belt, strikes the wicked, stands as a banner the nations seek, and his resting place is glorious.

l: animals (wolf, lamb, leopard, lion, etc.), The Book of Isaiah
s: A group of predators and prey (wolf, lamb, leopard, lion, bear, ox) lives together peacefully, led by a little child. Predators like the lion eat straw, and the young lie down together while children play safely near the cobra's and viper's dens.

l: holy mountain (the LORD's holy mountain), The Book of Isaiah
s: The LORD's holy mountain is a place free of hurt or destruction and full of knowledge of the LORD. There the LORD of Armies hosts a feast for all peoples, and his hand rests there.

l: remnant of the LORD's people, The Book of Isaiah
s: The remnant of the LORD's people, dispersed in Assyria, Egypt and other lands, will be recovered a second time. A highway will be made from Assyria, like Israel's from Egypt, and they will take root downward and bear fruit upward.

l: Edom, The Book of Isaiah
s: Edom is a land placed under the LORD's curse, its people called his cursed people. It suffers slaughter, including at Bozrah, then its streams become pitch and its dust sulfur, burning unquenched with smoke rising forever. Nobles come to nothing, thorns overgrow its fortresses, and it lies waste and impassable across generations, inhabited only by jackals, ostriches and other wild creatures.

l: Moab, The Book of Isaiah
s: Moab is a proud nation and land, with cities such as Ar, Kir Hareseth, Nebo and Medeba, whose destruction is foretold. In Chapter 15 it is laid waste in a single night; people wail, armed men tremble, nobles flee, and the land withers. In Chapter 16 it is likened to scattered birds, mourns ruined vineyards, and its prayers at the high place and sanctuary fail. In Chapter 25 it is trodden down like straw in dunghill water, its pride humbled, its boastings proven worthless, and its high fortress brought to dust, with downfall coming within three years.

l: righteous reign of the shoot, The Book of Isaiah
s: The shoot's rule is marked by judgment based on righteousness and equity rather than appearances, favoring the poor and humble and striking down the wicked. It is accompanied by peace among animals and people, with no hurt or destruction on the LORD's holy mountain, because the earth will be full of the knowledge of the LORD as the waters cover the sea.

l: gathering of the remnant, The Book of Isaiah
s: includes outcasts of Israel [from four corners of the earth] In that day the Lord will set his hand a second time to recover his people's remnant and will raise a banner for the nations to assemble Israel's outcasts and Judah's dispersed from the four corners of the earth. The LORD will remove barriers by splitting the River into seven streams and will make a highway for the remnant to return.

l: inhabitant of Zion, The Book of Isaiah
s: is_located_in Zion The inhabitant of Zion is addressed in the final verse and commanded to cry aloud and shout. The reason given is that the Holy One of Israel is great among them.

l: salvation, The Book of Isaiah
s: has_source wells of salvation [water drawn with joy] Salvation is identified with God, who is said to be the speaker's salvation and to have become it. It is also pictured as wells from which people will joyfully draw water.

l: Babylon, The Book of Isaiah
s: Babylon is a city and kingdom called the glory of kingdoms and the beauty of the Chaldeans' pride. The records trace its arc through Isaiah. First, it is foretold to be overthrown like Sodom and Gomorrah, never inhabited again, and left to wild animals, its time near. Next, the LORD of Armies vows to rise against it, cut off its name, remnant, son and son's son, and sweep it with the broom of destruction, leaving it to the porcupine and pools of water. Then a watchman announces it fallen, its gods' engraved images broken to the ground. Hezekiah calls it a far country, and Isaiah prophesies that his treasures and some sons, made eunuchs, will be carried there. Finally, the one whom the LORD loves is named as acting against Babylon and the Chaldeans, and the people are told to flee. Its overall course is from pride to prophesied desolation.

l: LORD of Armies, The Book of Isaiah
s: LORD of Armies is a divine figure, called Lord and God, who commands armies and acts in judgment and salvation. The records open with him mustering the nations' army and his consecrated ones and mighty men for battle, vowing to punish the world's evil, end the arrogance of the proud, shake heaven and earth, and stir up the Medes against Babylon. Next he brings a day of confusion in the valley of vision, declares the people's iniquity unforgiven until death, and removes Shebna in favor of Eliakim. He is then praised as faithful, having done wonders planned long ago and being a stronghold and refuge to the poor and needy. He swallows up death forever, wipes away tears, and removes his people's reproach, while they await his salvation. He distresses and besieges Ariel, visiting it with thunder, earthquake, whirlwind and fire, sends deep sleep on prophets and seers, and promises a marvelous work, redeeming Abraham and acting for Jacob's house. Finally, he anoints a speaker to proclaim good news and liberty, declares he loves justice and hates robbery and iniquity, rewards his people in truth, and makes an everlasting covenant. Overall he is warrior-judge, refuge, and covenant-maker.

l: Medes, The Book of Isaiah
s: The Medes are a people the LORD stirs up against Babylon's people; indifferent to silver and gold, they are ruthless warriors whose bows dash young men down and who spare neither children nor the unborn.

l: day of the LORD, The Book of Isaiah
s: The day of the LORD is an imminent event coming as destruction from the Almighty, cruel with wrath and fierce anger. It desolates the land and destroys sinners, while stars, sun, and moon lose light and heavens and earth tremble.

l: army of the nations (mustered by the LORD), The Book of Isaiah
s: An army of gathered kingdoms of nations, mustered by the LORD of Armies, is heard as a great uproar in the mountains; coming from a far country, they serve as weapons of his indignation to destroy the whole land.

l: inhabitants of Babylon's land, The Book of Isaiah
s: The inhabitants of Babylon's land face the day of the LORD: told to wail, their hands go feeble and hearts melt, and they writhe like a woman in labor. They flee like hunted gazelles to their own lands, but all found or captured are killed by the sword.

l: Jacob, The Book of Isaiah
s: Jacob, also called Israel and Jeshurun, is the LORD's chosen people and servant, addressed throughout these records as both a collective nation (the house of Jacob) and, in the final chapter, a figure tied to a servant who speaks. The records open with compassion and restoration: Jacob will be joined by foreigners and returned to his own land. Then comes a darker picture. Jacob's glory will be made thin, leaving only a few gleanings like olives on a shaken tree. He is a plundered people, robbed and captive with no deliverer, and the text says this happened because he sinned, would not walk in the LORD's ways, and disobeyed the law. He complains that his way is hidden from the LORD, yet he is accused of not calling on him, of neglecting offerings, and of wearying him with sins. He is called obstinate, treacherous, and a transgressor from the womb, and is warned he will be made a curse. Alongside this runs a steady current of grace. He was created, redeemed, called by name, and is precious and honored. He was chosen and refined in the furnace of affliction, and the LORD has not forgotten him. His sins are blotted out and his iniquity forgiven, so that idolatrous altars fall. He is promised the outpouring of the Spirit, offspring who take his name, and a future in which he will no longer be ashamed, will take root, blossom, and fill the world with fruit, and his children will sanctify the Holy One of Jacob. He is told to leave Babylon, and it is proclaimed that the LORD has redeemed his servant. The arc ends with the servant's voice: called from the womb, his mouth made like a sharp sword, hidden in the LORD's quiver as a polished shaft. He laments laboring in vain but trusts the LORD for justice. Raising up Jacob is called too light a task, so he is appointed a light to the nations, the LORD's salvation to earth's end, and a covenant for the people. Though despised by man and abhorred by the nation, kings will rise and worship. Overall the records move from promise, through judgment and rebuke, to redemption and a widening, universal purpose.

l: king of Babylon, The Book of Isaiah
s: The king of Babylon is mocked in a parable as an oppressor who struck peoples in wrath. Proud, he vowed to ascend to heaven and rival the Most High. He is instead brought down to Sheol and the pit, denied burial because he destroyed his land and killed his people, and his offspring are to be slaughtered.

l: Philistia, The Book of Isaiah
s: Philistia is warned not to rejoice that the rod that struck it is broken, since worse will arise from the serpent's root. Its root will die by famine, its remnant be killed, and it must howl as smoke comes from the north.

l: destruction of Moab, The Book of Isaiah
s: occurs_in a night [Ar and Kir of Moab laid waste] Ar of Moab and Kir of Moab are laid waste and brought to nothing in a single night. The waters of Nimrim become desolate and the grass withers, and survivors carry off their stored goods over the brook of the willows. The waters of Dimon are full of blood, with yet more promised on Dimon and a lion on those who escape and on the remnant of the land.

l: mourning of Moab, The Book of Isaiah
s: Moab's mourning is a nationwide lament: people go up to Bayith, Dibon, and the high places to weep over Nebo and Medeba, with heads shaved, beards cut, and sackcloth worn in streets and on housetops. The wailing echoes through Heshbon, Elealeh, Jahaz, and to Moab's borders, and the speaker's heart cries out.

l: outcasts and fugitive (Moabite refugees), The Book of Isaiah
s: is_to_be_sheltered_from destroyer [hiding place requested] The outcasts and fugitive are those for whom shelter is requested: they are to be hidden, not betrayed, and allowed to dwell with Zion. Moab is to find a hiding place from the face of the destroyer.

l: righteous king (throne in the tent of David), The Book of Isaiah
s: A promised righteous king whose throne is established in loving kindness and who sits in truth in the tent of David. He judges, seeks justice, and is swift to do righteousness once oppressors are gone; later he reigns in righteousness alongside just princes.

l: Moab's pride, The Book of Isaiah
s: has_component arrogance and wrath It is reported that Moab is very proud, marked by arrogance, pride and wrath. His boastings are declared to be nothing.

l: Moab's coming downfall within three years, The Book of Isaiah
s: The LORD announces Moab's downfall within three years, counted like a contract worker's; its glory and great multitude will be held in contempt, leaving only a very small, feeble remnant.

l: children of Israel, The Book of Isaiah
s: The children of Israel, also called Jacob and Jeshurun, are portrayed as both a people and a servant figure of the LORD. They are offspring of Abraham, chosen and upheld by the LORD, yet deeply revolted against him, making idols of silver and gold with their own hands, and described as blind and deaf, seeing without observing and hearing without listening. Called a worm, they are told not to fear, since the LORD holds their right hand and will make them a new threshing instrument that threshes mountains and hills. The servant has the LORD's Spirit and brings justice faithfully and gently, not breaking a bruised reed; he is a covenant for the people and a light for the nations, opening blind eyes and freeing prisoners. Early passages mention their glory as a comparison for Damascus's remnant and call them to return and cast away their idols. Later they are named the LORD's witnesses that there is no other God, promised they will not be forgotten, their transgressions blotted out like a cloud, and redeemed, so that heaven and earth sing as the LORD glorifies himself in Israel.

l: many peoples and nations, The Book of Isaiah
s: Many peoples and nations roar and rush like seas and mighty waters, but the LORD rebukes them, and they flee far off, scattered like chaff and whirling dust before wind.

l: plunderers (those who plunder us), The Book of Isaiah
s: has_portion terror and disappearance [gone before morning] Those who plunder and rob the speaker's people bring terror at evening but are gone before morning. This is called their portion and their lot.

l: people of Israel, The Book of Isaiah
s: The people of Israel are accused of forgetting the God of their salvation and the rock of their strength, planting pleasant plants and foreign seedlings whose harvest flees in grief. Yet in that day they will look to their Maker, the Holy One of Israel, disregarding altars, while strong cities become desolate.

l: judgment on Damascus, The Book of Isaiah
s: is_called burden of Damascus The judgment is announced as a burden in which Damascus becomes a ruinous heap and its cities are abandoned to flocks. It also ends the fortress of Ephraim and the kingdom of Damascus and the remnant of Syria, and it is tied to a wider reckoning that thins Jacob's glory and turns people from idols.

l: Ethiopia, The Book of Isaiah
s: Ethiopia is a place serving as a sign and an expectation that dismays Egypt; its exiles, young and old, are led away naked and barefoot by Assyria's king, and it submits to Cyrus.

l: nation tall and smooth, The Book of Isaiah
s: A nation, awesome from its beginning, that measures out and treads down, with land divided by rivers. It receives ambassadors via swift messengers in papyrus vessels, and later brings a present to the LORD of Armies at Mount Zion.

l: land of the rustling of wings, The Book of Isaiah
s: A land addressed with 'Ah', located beyond the rivers of Ethiopia; it sends ambassadors by sea in papyrus vessels, bidding swift messengers go to a tall, smooth nation.

l: harvest, The Book of Isaiah
s: The harvest is the setting for the LORD's stillness, likened to a cloud of dew in the heat of harvest. Before it, when the blossom is over and the flower becomes a ripening grape, the LORD will cut off the sprigs and branches.

l: sprigs and spreading branches (of the vine), The Book of Isaiah
s: The vine's sprigs and spreading branches are cut off by the LORD with pruning hooks before the harvest, once the flower becomes a ripening grape, then left together for mountain birds and earth's animals to eat through summer and winter.

l: present (brought to the LORD of Armies), The Book of Isaiah
s: A present is brought to the LORD of Armies at that time by the tall, smooth nation that measures out and treads down, delivered to Mount Zion, the place of the LORD's name.

l: Egyptians, The Book of Isaiah
s: The Egyptians are a people shown in two stages. In Chapter 19 they fall into infighting, lose their spirit, turn to idols and wizards, are handed to a fierce king, and fear Judah. Then, in that day, they cry to the LORD, know him, worship, are healed, and worship with the Assyrians. In Chapter 31 they are declared men, not God, with horses of flesh, and will stumble and be consumed with those they help.

l: Pharaoh, The Book of Isaiah
s: Pharaoh is a ruler whose counselors' advice has become foolish; the rebellious rely on his strength, which the LORD declares will become their shame.

l: burden of Egypt (judgment and restoration), The Book of Isaiah
s: concerns Egypt [judgment followed by healing] The burden of Egypt opens with judgment: civil strife, a cruel ruler, a failing Nile, and foolish counselors in Zoan and Memphis misled by a perverse spirit. It turns in 'that day' to restoration, with Egyptian worship of the LORD, deliverance from oppressors, striking and healing, and a shared blessing with Assyria and Israel.

l: captives and exiles of Egypt and Ethiopia, The Book of Isaiah
s: Captives of Egypt and exiles of Ethiopia, young and old, are foretold to be led away by Assyria's king, naked and barefoot with buttocks uncovered, shaming Egypt.

l: inhabitants (of this coast land), The Book of Isaiah
s: fled_for_help_to Ethiopia [seeking deliverance from the king of Assyria] The inhabitants of this coast land will say in that day that Egypt and Ethiopia were their expectation, where they fled for help to be delivered from the king of Assyria. They will ask how they themselves will escape.

l: Isaiah's walking naked and barefoot, The Book of Isaiah
s: At the LORD's command, Isaiah removed sackcloth and sandals and walked naked and barefoot for three years, a sign and wonder foreshadowing Egypt's and Ethiopia's captives being led away by Assyria.

l: Dumah, The Book of Isaiah
s: Dumah is the subject of a burden in Chapter 21: someone calls from Seir asking the watchman about the night, and the watchman answers that morning and night come, urging further inquiry.

l: Arabia, The Book of Isaiah
s: Arabia is the subject of a burden: Dedanite caravans will lodge in its thickets, while Tema's people are said to have given water and bread to fugitives fleeing swords, bow and battle.

l: Kedar, The Book of Isaiah
s: Kedar is a group with glory and mighty archers; the LORD declares that within a year its glory will fail and its remaining archers will be few.

l: watchman (set by the Lord), The Book of Isaiah
s: A watchman appointed by the Lord's command to declare what he sees and listen attentively. He stands on the watchtower day and night, reports pairs of horsemen, announces Babylon's fall, and answers Seir's question about the night in the Dumah burden.

l: speaker (the prophet), The Book of Isaiah
s: receives_message_from the LORD [declares what he heard from the LORD of Armies] The speaker says a grievous vision has been declared to him and describes his anguish, pain like a woman in labor, failing hearing and sight, a fluttering heart, and twilight turned into trembling. He receives the Lord's instruction to set a watchman and says he has declared what he heard from the LORD of Armies. He also relays the Lord's word about Kedar.

l: burden of the wilderness of the sea, The Book of Isaiah
s: A burden in Chapter 21 arriving like southern whirlwinds from an awesome wilderness: it shows a grievous vision of the treacherous man and destroyer, calls Elam to attack, ends Media's sighing, and declares Babylon fallen.

l: valley of vision, The Book of Isaiah
s: The valley of vision is the subject of a burden: a tumultuous, joyous city whose slain did not die by the sword and whose rulers fled and were bound. It then suffers a day of confusion and treading down from the Lord, with broken walls.

l: Shebna, The Book of Isaiah
s: Shebna is a royal official, treasurer over the house and later scribe, who carved himself a high tomb in the rock. In Chapter 22 he is condemned as a disgrace to his lord's house and prophesied to be removed from office and hurled like a ball into a large country to die. In Chapter 36, as scribe, he joins Eliakim and Joah meeting Rabshakeh, stays silent, and reports to Hezekiah in torn clothes.

l: Eliakim, The Book of Isaiah
s: Eliakim, son of Hilkiah, is called the LORD's servant. He is set to succeed Shebna, receiving his robe, belt and government, becoming a father to Jerusalem's inhabitants and Judah's house, and carrying the key of David's house, opening and shutting without hindrance. He is likened to a nail fastened in a sure place, bearing his father's house's glory, though that nail is finally said to give way and be cut down. Later, as the official over the household under Hezekiah, he meets Rabshakeh, asks him to speak Aramaic, stays silent at the king's command, and reports to Hezekiah with torn clothes.

l: inhabitants of Jerusalem, The Book of Isaiah
s: has_state slain not by sword [not dead in battle] The inhabitants shout in a joyous city while their rulers have fled. They look to armor, gather water, and break down houses for defense but do not look to the one who planned it long ago. Called to mourning, they feast instead, and are told their iniquity will not be forgiven until they die. Eliakim is to be a father to them.

l: siege preparations (Jerusalem's defense), The Book of Isaiah
s: Jerusalem's defense preparations in Chapter 22: the people note the many breaches in David's city, gather the lower pool's waters, inspect armor in the house of the forest, count and break down houses to fortify the wall, and build a reservoir between the two walls. The text faults them for not looking to God, who planned it long ago.

l: feasting (in the day of mourning), The Book of Isaiah
s: A feasting event on a day when GOD of Armies called for weeping, mourning, and sackcloth. The people instead celebrated, killing cattle and sheep, eating and drinking, saying 'tomorrow we will die.' The LORD declares this iniquity unforgiven until their death.

l: Tyre, The Book of Isaiah
s: Tyre is an ancient, joyous city of merchant princes, giver of crowns and market of nations, the target of a burden in Chapter 23. It is laid waste, with no house or entrance remaining, and forgotten for seventy years. Then, when the LORD visits her, she returns to her wages and trades with all kingdoms, like a forgotten prostitute seeking remembrance. Finally, her merchandise and earnings become holiness to the LORD.

l: Sidon, The Book of Isaiah
s: Sidon is a coastal seafaring place whose merchants once replenished the coast's inhabitants. It is told to be ashamed, and its daughter, an oppressed virgin, is told she will rejoice no more and find no rest, even fleeing to Kittim.

l: seventy years of Tyre's oblivion, The Book of Isaiah
s: has_duration seventy years [according to the days of one king] Tyre will be forgotten for seventy years, according to the days of one king. At the end of that period the LORD will visit her, and she will return to her wages and trade with all the kingdoms of the world.

l: destruction of Tyre, The Book of Isaiah
s: has_cause LORD of Armies Tyre is described as laid waste, with no house and no entering in, a result the LORD of Armies planned to bring contempt on the pride of glory. The report of it will cause anguish in Egypt, and the ships of Tarshish and the coast dwellers are told to howl, be still, or flee.
